source: cross-examiner verdicts from the research fleets (one agent per contested claim, both lenses)

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads as: the six MP THR plants supplied take-home ration to 49.58 lakh registered beneficiaries over 2018–21. Neither source dates 49.58 lakh as a 2018–21 figure. The Quint gives it as a snapshot: "The most stark irregularities were found in the Take Home Ration (THR) programme in 2021, which was aimed at providing nourishing meals for 49.58 lakh registered women and children" (34.69 lakh children aged 6 months to 3 years, 14.25 lakh pregnant or lactating mothers, 64,000 out-of-school adolescent girls). Scroll says only "a programme under which 49.58 lakh children and women are registered". The 2018–21 window is the audit period, not a registration count. I could not confirm when the SHG-federation plants began production, so whether the six plants ran for all of 2018–21 is unverified (web search budget exhausted). That gap should be recorded.
verdicts.identityTest: The six plant locations (Sagar, Badi, Mandla, Dhar, Rewa, Shivpuri) appear only in Scroll. The Quint says only "six ration manufacturing plants" and names none. Scroll uses the six names in a different context: "Six plants in the areas of Sagar, Badi, Mandla, Dhar, Rewa and Shivpuri said they supplied 821 metric tons of rations that cost Rs 4.95 crore but did not have the capacity to produce at such a large scale, the report claimed." Scroll also says the network is larger than six: "Rs 141 crore was paid in advance to the Madhya Pradesh State Rural Livelihood Mission for establishing seven plants" (Scroll attributing this to the Hindustan Times). So six is the audited subset, and the whole beneficiary base cannot be credited to these six. The operator node is "MPSRLM-linked SHG federations / MP Agro". Scroll links MPSRLM to the ₹141 cr advance. It mentions MP Agro only as the body whose "investigation" found the vehicle-registration errors were "clerical". It never calls MP Agro an implementing agency or plant operator. No federation, society registration or CIN is named in either source.
verdicts.baseRate: Centralised THR production through state-designated plants, increasingly run by SHG federations under the 2017 SNP guidelines and NRLM convergence, is the normal ICDS arrangement across states (compare the Maharashtra 2016 tender control in the same file). So an award of a THR supply mandate to a state or SHG body tells you nothing about wrongdoing on its own; almost every state has one. The only thing that could set this edge apart is the audit's capacity and transport findings, and those sit in the separate audit claim, not here.
verdicts.denialFound: This is not a denial of this edge. It is the state's response to the audit it comes from. Scroll, citing the Hindustan Times, quotes WCD Additional Chief Secretary Ashok Shah: "The transport of THR is mentioned by motorcycle, car, auto and tanker instead of trucks ... it was found in MP Agro's investigation that the above errors have been made in clerical form." He also called the report "an interim one". Source: https://scroll.in/latest/1032051/madhya-pradesh-large-scale-irregularities-found-in-nutrition-scheme-claims-audit-report. I found no response from MPSRLM or the plant federations, and there is no record that they were asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: MP WCD runs a statewide THR programme with about 49.58 lakh registered beneficiaries (as of 2021). Production is spread across about seven plants that MPSRLM set up with a ₹141 cr advance. The AG's draft audit examined six of them. The edge simply records a state supply arrangement. Read innocently it implies neither exclusivity nor that these six plants supplied every beneficiary.
verdicts.reason: This claim joins two separate facts from the sources. Fact 1 is the size of the statewide programme (49.58 lakh registered, per The Quint "in 2021"). Fact 2 is Scroll's list of six plants, which appears only in a sentence saying they claimed to supply 821 MT (₹4.95 cr) beyond their capacity. The label merges them into "six plants supplied THR for 49.58 lakh beneficiaries, 2018–21", which neither source says. Scroll itself refers to seven plants, and The Quint dates the 49.58 lakh figure to 2021, not 2018–21. The underlying award relationship (MP WCD/MPSRLM to the THR plants) is supported at reported tier. The label as written is not.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Replace lab with: "MP WCD's THR programme (49.58 lakh registered beneficiaries, 2021) was produced through about seven MPSRLM-established plants (₹141 cr advanced). The AG draft audit (2018–21) examined six, at Sagar, Badi, Mandla, Dhar, Rewa and Shivpuri." 2. Put the six plant names on Scroll only; The Quint does not name them. Attribute the ₹141 cr / seven-plant figure to Scroll citing the Hindustan Times. 3. In d, remove "MP Agro Industries Development Corporation" as an implementing agency per Scroll. Scroll names MP Agro only as the body that investigated the transport errors. Keep MP Agro in the operator label only if a source that says so is added. 4. from/to: keep 2018–2021 as the audit period, but state that 49.58 lakh is a 2021 registration figure, not a 2018–21 total. 5. Record as a gap that the start date of SHG-federation production at the six plants was not verified. 6. Tier stays reported (Scroll citing NDTV/HT citing an unpublished draft audit; The Quint accessed the document). The upgradeIf is fine as written.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: the AG (MP) draft audit (s: cag) flagged THR irregularities for 2018–21, and NDTV reported it on Sunday 4 Sep 2022. Scroll and The Quint followed on 5 Sep, and ThePrint/PTI carried the state's denial on 7 Sep. The audit period (2018–21) overlaps the period the findings describe, so there is no chronology break. Two small problems. 'Sep 2022' is when the report leaked, not when it was issued. The draft's own date is unknown. The label should say 'draft AG (MP) audit, reported 4–5 Sep 2022'. There is also no evidence that the draft was ever finalised or tabled as a CAG report. The state said the AG had asked for factual replies within two weeks before deciding whether to include the findings.
verdicts.identityTest:
This test fails for the edge as drawn. The target node is ngo:mp-thr-plant-operators, but the sources pin only some of the findings on the plants.

Findings that are about the plants:
- The ₹6.94 cr transport finding. Scroll: 'trucks were used in six manufacturing plants for transporting 1,125.64 metric tons of rations costing Rs 6.94 crore ... the vehicles were registered as motorcycles, cars, auto rickshaws and tankers'.
- The ₹58 cr over-capacity production finding. Quint: 'ration manufacturing plants ... reporting a production rate which was well beyond their permitted capacity ... Rs 58 crore was found to be fabricated'.

Findings that are about the WCD department, not the plants:
- The 36.08 lakh vs 9,000 girls figure. Quint: 'the School Education Department estimated that there were only 9,000 out-of-school girls in 2018-19, the WCD Department estimated the number to be 36.08 lakh'.
- The ₹110.83 cr figure. It is beneficiary-data manipulation tied to the WCD listing 63,748 girls at 49 centres where only 3 were registered.
- The ₹62.72 cr shortfall. It is a district-to-anganwadi distribution gap. PTI/ThePrint: 'eight districts had received 97,656 MT ... but in anganwadis only 86,377 MT was transported'. That is downstream of the plants.

The plant node also has no CIN, registration number or named federation (identity is all null). The sources name MPSRLM (₹141 cr advance) and MP Agro, not individual operators.

The predicate is also wrong. An unpublished draft AG observation is not 'enforce' (cancellation, suspension, freeze, investigation, sanction or debarment). It is an audit finding.
verdicts.baseRate: Not quantified. No web search budget was left, and the repo has no cross-state THR/ICDS audit table. Audit findings of inflated beneficiary counts and leakage in supplementary nutrition are commonly reported across many states, so on its own the finding does not single out MP or any ruling party. That is an impression, not a count. The symmetry control (the same THR/ICDS audit lens applied to states run by opposition parties) was not run and is not recorded in the file.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, and it is already recorded as contra c024. ThePrint/PTI, 7 Sep 2022, quoting MP Home Minister Narottam Mishra: 'Just because bills for transportation were not paid doesn't mean it (food material) was not transported'. He also said the report 'was not final' and cited a vehicle-number mismatch: 'MP 15 AV 3835' in the report vs 'MP 15 LA 3835' in department records (https://theprint.in/india/no-corruption-in-nutrition-scheme-ag-audit-report-not-final-mp-home-minister/1119984/). Scroll, citing Hindustan Times, quotes ACS (WCD) Ashok Shah: 'it was found in MP Agro's investigation that the above errors have been made in clerical form', and says the report is 'interim'. I found no response from the plant operators or SHG federations themselves. Whether they were asked is unknown.
verdicts.innocentReading:
The draft is a preliminary audit observation. At that stage the audited department has not yet sent its replies, and the AG had asked for factual information within two weeks. Some of the flags could fall away or shrink:
- The vehicle flags could be transcription errors in registration numbers (the state gives one specific example).
- The stock gap could reflect unpaid transport bills that were left out of the auditors' stock reconciliation.
- The 36.08 lakh vs 9,000 gap could reflect a late or poor WCD survey and mismatched definitions of 'out-of-school girls' between two departments, rather than deliberate fabrication by the plants.

Final CAG reports often drop or restate figures from such drafts.
verdicts.reason: I checked each figure against the sources, and every one matches. Scroll and The Quint both give 110.83, 6.94, 58, 62.72 and 36.08 lakh vs 9,000, all attributed to the NDTV-accessed 36-page AG draft. So the numbers are fine; the edge is not. The label attaches all five figures to 'MP THR plant operators' under an 'enforce' predicate. By the sources' own wording, three of the five (₹110.83 cr beneficiary-data manipulation, 36.08 lakh vs 9,000 girls, ₹62.72 cr district-to-anganwadi shortfall) are findings against the WCD department's identification and distribution, not the plants. Only the ₹6.94 cr transport and ₹58 cr over-capacity findings concern the six plants, and those plants are not identified beyond their locations (Sagar, Badi, Mandla, Dhar, Rewa, Shivpuri). A leaked, unfinalised draft audit is also not enforcement. On sourcing: Scroll and The Quint are not independent. Both rest on NDTV's access to the draft, so 'reported' is the right ceiling. ThePrint/PTI confirms that the report exists, the vehicle finding and the 97,656/86,377 MT gap, but none of the rupee amounts.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Split the edge in two.
   - (a) s: cag (better a node for AG MP / IA&AD), t: ministry:mp-wcd. Carries ₹110.83 cr beneficiary-data manipulation; 36.08 lakh (WCD) vs 9,000 (School Education Dept) out-of-school girls, 2018-19; 3 registered vs 63,748 listed at 49 anganwadis; ₹62.72 cr shortfall, where 8 districts received 97,656 MT and 86,377 MT reached anganwadis.
   - (b) t: ngo:mp-thr-plant-operators. Carries only ₹6.94 cr / 1,125.64 MT transport by vehicles registered as motorcycles, cars, autos and tankers (add 'tankers'), and ₹58 cr production beyond capacity, using raw-material and electricity comparisons, at six plants.
2. Change pred from 'enforce' to an audit-finding predicate, or to 'analytic'/'law' as the schema allows. A draft AG observation is not enforcement. If 'enforce' must stay, write 'draft audit observation, not adjudicated' in d.
3. Relabel as 'Draft AG (MP) audit, reported by NDTV 4 Sep 2022 (Scroll/Quint 5 Sep)'. Note that Scroll and The Quint both derive from NDTV and are not independent.
4. Keep tier 'reported'. Do not upgrade unless a tabled CAG report with the same figures is found.
5. Add to d that the ₹141 cr unrecovered advance went to MPSRLM for seven plants. That is the one finding that names the plants' parent body.
6. Keep contra c024 and record that the plant operators themselves were not quoted: 'asked/not asked unknown'.
7. Add a symmetry note that the same THR/ICDS audit test has not been run on opposition-ruled states.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. Restated claim: INC (with CPI(M) and TMC) alleged a ₹100+ cr "poshan scam" and demanded a central-agency probe, around 5 Sep 2022. Scroll's datePublished is 2022-09-05T10:10+05:30 and The Quint's is 2022-09-05T14:52+05:30. Babul Supriyo was in the TMC by then (he joined in Sep 2021). Sitaram Yechury was CPI(M) General Secretary (2015 to 2024). Chouhan was CM and held WCD, so the target existed at that date. from=2022-09-05 is correct. The denial (c026, ThePrint, 7 Sep 2022) comes after the allegation.
verdicts.identityTest: Partly fails. Each actor made a different statement, and the claim merges them under INC. Scroll: "Opposition leaders have demanded an inquiry by a central agency into the alleged scam. 'Why not CBI for this?' asked Trinamool Congress leader Babul Supriyo". Yechury (CPI(M)) "asked if central agencies would take any action". Congress's own statement was different: "The Congress tweeted that the Shivraj Singh Chouhan-led government had earlier conspired to 'ruin the future of youth' by committing the Vyapam scam and was now 'killing the rights of poor children and pregnant women' through the latest alleged corruption scandal." ThePrint (7 Sep) says Congress "demanded the resignation of Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, who heads the WCD department". It does not say Congress asked for a central-agency probe. So the probe demand belongs to TMC and CPI(M), not INC. The ₹100+ cr figure (₹110.83 cr) comes from the AG draft as reported by NDTV and The Quint, not from anything Congress said. The phrase "poshan scam" appears in neither cited source (0 matches in Scroll or The Quint). The Quint says nothing at all about Congress, CPI(M), TMC or any probe demand, so it supports only the amount.
verdicts.baseRate: Close to 100% and so non-discriminating. Opposition parties in India almost always call a leaked adverse AG/CAG draft a "scam" and ask for a CBI or central-agency probe. The same pattern shows up with the parties reversed: the BJP demanded CBI probes in Congress- or TMC-run states (for example the Bengal ration and recruitment cases). An opposition demand tells us nothing about wrongdoing on its own. At most it records the political reaction.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes. ThePrint, 7 Sep 2022 (https://theprint.in/india/no-corruption-in-nutrition-scheme-ag-audit-report-not-final-mp-home-minister/1119984/). MP Home Minister Narottam Mishra: "There were no irregularities in the poshan-aahar programme" and "The report in question was not final." This is already recorded as contra c026. Scroll also quotes the state's reply to the audit: "it was found in MP Agro's investigation that the above errors have been made in clerical form."
verdicts.innocentReading: This is ordinary opposition messaging after a leaked draft AG audit. The state called the draft interim and put some findings down to clerical and transcription errors. The AG itself asked the state government for an independent-agency investigation. No FIR, EOW/Lokayukta case or central-agency action followed on the record in hand. A demand from an opposition party is not an enforcement action.
verdicts.reason: Two problems, and either one is enough to refute. (1) Wrong predicate. The CONTRACT defines `enforce` as agency→subject (cancellation, suspension, freeze, investigation, sanction, debarment). A political party demanding a probe is none of these, so the edge implies an enforcement action that never happened. The CONTRACT also bars "alleged" as a stand-in predicate, and no predicate fits a political demand. (2) The sources back a looser version of the claim. INC did not demand a central-agency probe in the cited sources. TMC (Supriyo: "Why not CBI for this?") and CPI(M) (Yechury) did. INC made a Vyapam comparison and, per ThePrint, demanded Chouhan's resignation. Neither source attributes the ₹100+ cr figure or the phrase "poshan scam" to Congress. The Quint does not mention the opposition at all. The underlying facts (an opposition outcry and a demand for a central probe) are real and reported by Scroll with named quotes. They belong in a node description or the narrative at tier reported, not as an INC→mp-wcd enforce edge.
verdicts.corrections: Kill c025 as an edge. Its contra c026 then has nothing to attach to; point it at the audit claim or the narrative instead. Keep the content as text at tier `reported` with Scroll as the only source: "After the leaked AG draft (5 Sep 2022), TMC's Babul Supriyo asked 'Why not CBI for this?' and CPI(M)'s Sitaram Yechury asked whether central agencies would act; Congress likened it to Vyapam and (ThePrint, 7 Sep 2022) demanded CM Chouhan's resignation." Remove The Quint as a source for the opposition statements; it supports only the ₹110.83 cr AG-draft figure. Drop the quotation marks around 'poshan scam', since neither cited source uses the phrase, and attribute ₹100+ cr to the AG draft, not to Congress. In the party:inc node, change the d line "With CPI(M), TMC and others demanded a central-agency investigation citing the Vyapam precedent" to separate the Congress statement (Vyapam comparison, resignation demand) from the TMC/CPI(M) CBI demand. Apply the same wording fix to the narrative claim at line ~2499 ("₹100+ crore 'poshan scam'"). Files: /home/user/india-corporate-intelligence/research/raw/ngo/darpan-welfare-join.json (c025 ~line 1954, party:inc node ~line 1349, narrative ~line 2499).

verdicts.dateTest: Stated as: CAG found that SHGs supplied hot cooked meals to MP anganwadis during the audit period ending Mar 2024, and this was reported in Jul 2026. The source says "during its audit of the establishment and functioning of anganwadi centres for the period ending March 2024." FPJ metadata gives dateModified 2026-07-22T22:54 IST and datePublished 2026-07-23T05:00 IST, so the record's "22 Jul 2026" is fine. There is no tenure question because the actor is an institution (CAG) and the target is an aggregate of SHG suppliers. One caveat: `from: 2024-03-31` is when the audit period ended, not when anything happened. The supply took place at unstated points before that date. The report's tabling date (about Jul 2026) is not given in the article.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor, CAG, is named by the source: "The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has flagged irregularities in the supply of hot cooked meals (HCM) under the Women and Child Development Department." The target node `ngo:mp-hcm-shg-suppliers` is an unnamed aggregate. The article names no SHG, registration number or kitchen operator, so no entity-level identity can be checked. The article also does not say the 13 SHGs with no premises are a subset of the 54 unregistered SHGs. The 13 are placed in Alirajpur, Sehore and Tikamgarh, while the 54 are in Mandla, Burhanpur, Datia, Sehore, Shajapur and Sheopur, and only Sehore is in both lists. Merging them into one node suggests an overlap the source does not state. The label keeps the two findings apart with a semicolon, which is acceptable.
verdicts.baseRate: This finding does not pick out MP or any one SHG. CAG and AG performance audits of ICDS/SNP in many states (MP's THR audit in 2022, plus Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Karnataka and UP) regularly report weak supplier eligibility, missing stock registers and breaches of catering norms. Record-keeping failures of this kind probably show up in most state ICDS audits. The more specific points (13 addresses with no kitchen or office, male non-members cooking) are sharper, but they are one audit's findings on a sample of districts (7 of 13 test-checked). On symmetry: the same lens applied to an audit of an opposition-run state would produce the same kind of edge (CAG enforce -> supplier aggregate). The claim names no party, family, religion or ethnicity as the actor.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; the MP WCD department was not asked. The FPJ article carries no response from the government or the department. The CAG report text (which usually includes the government's reply) could not be found on cag.gov.in in this pass, and the web-search budget was used up. The absence is already recorded in c029.
verdicts.innocentReading: "Unregistered" may mean the SHGs had not registered under the specific state or NRLM mechanism the scheme requires, not that they were fictitious. District officers may have chosen centralised kitchens to deliver meals in remote tribal districts (Alirajpur, Sheopur, Mandla) where there were not enough qualifying SHGs. Paying hired cooks and keeping no stock registers is a compliance failure, not proof that meals were never delivered. The ₹8.1 cr is the value of supplies from non-compliant SHGs, not an assessed loss or amount diverted.
verdicts.reason: The source confirms every element of the label almost word for word: "54 unregistered self-help groups (SHGs) were engaged in supplying HCM in seven of the 13 test-checked districts... These SHGs supplied meals worth Rs 8.1 crore to 252 anganwadi centres," and "13 SHGs in Alirajpur, Sehore and Tikamgarh had neither kitchens nor offices at the addresses mentioned in bills." The period ("ending March 2024"), the actor (CAG) and the amount (Rs 8.1 crore, so no currency conversion) all match. The CAG report itself was not located, so this rests on one credible outlet reporting an audit document, which is the definition of `reported`. The tier is right. The claim frames the ₹8.1 cr as supply value, not loss, and implies no wrongdoing beyond what the audit says. Only minor fixes to the description are needed.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Field `d`: the district list is garbled. The article says "seven of the 13 test-checked districts" but names only six (Mandla, Burhanpur, Datia, Sehore, Shajapur, Sheopur). The seventh is unnamed in the source. The no-premises finding covers Alirajpur, Sehore AND Tikamgarh; the current `d` leaves out Sehore and implies Alirajpur/Tikamgarh make up the seventh district. Suggested wording: "54 unregistered SHGs in 7 of 13 test-checked districts (six named: Mandla, Burhanpur, Datia, Sehore, Shajapur, Sheopur); separately, 13 SHGs in Alirajpur, Sehore and Tikamgarh had no kitchen/office at billed addresses." 2) Add to `d` that the source does not say whether the 13 are among the 54. 3) Add that the ₹4.11 cr for 132 AWCs relates to the centralised kitchens linked to the 13 SHGs; the source does not tie it to breaches of the 10-AWC norm. The current `d` says "132 AWCs fed from centralised kitchens for ₹4.11 cr against the 10-AWC-per-SHG norm", which conflates two separate points. 4) `from: 2024-03-31` should be annotated as the end of the audit period, or the report/reporting date (2026-07-22) added as the event date. 5) Keep `upgradeIf` (CAG report PDF). Add `upgradeIf`: the government reply in the report, or a second outlet.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: MP WCD (through its district programme officers) paid 54 unregistered SHGs ₹8.1 cr for hot cooked meals to 252 anganwadi centres, in the CAG audit period ending March 2024. The source is FPJ, 22 Jul 2026, and it says "for the period ending March 2024". The "to": "2024-03-31" field matches. The actor is a state department, so no tenure window applies. The audit period and the reporting date are consistent with each other. Passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The source names the payer only as district programme officers, who work under MP WCD, which is the ICDS implementing department. So ministry:mp-wcd is correct as the source node. The target is a collective node (ngo:mp-hcm-shg-suppliers, ty=group) standing for the 54 SHGs that the article counts but does not name. The node's label and sub say this correctly ("CAG test-check sample", 7 of 13 districts). No individual registration numbers exist to check, and the claim does not assert any. What "unregistered" means (not registered under which Act or portal) is not specified in the article. That ambiguity is already covered by c028's killIf. Passes, with that caveat.
verdicts.baseRate: Weak ICDS supplementary-nutrition compliance, with SHGs or mahila mandals that are ineligible or fronts, shows up again and again in CAG and state audits across both BJP- and opposition-ruled states. Maharashtra (Vaishnorani, c031) and Karnataka/UP take-home-ration contractor findings are examples. So the property does not discriminate as evidence of anything MP-specific or partisan. That does not matter here: this edge is a sized money flow taken from an audit finding, not an inference drawn from how rare the finding is. The symmetry control holds. The same lens applied to a CAG finding in an opposition-run state would give an identical edge. No family, religion or ethnicity is framed as the actor.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. The FPJ article carries no response from the WCD department or the state government (WebFetch: "The article contains no government or WCD department response"). Whether anyone was asked is not recorded, and sibling edge c029 already says so. CAG reports normally print the government's reply, but the report PDF was not located. A new web search could not be run because the session's search budget was exhausted.
verdicts.innocentReading: District officers used local women's groups that had not completed formal registration or empanelment (for example on the state SHG/NRLM portal) so that meals kept reaching the anganwadis. This is a compliance and documentation lapse, not diversion, and the ₹8.1 cr may correspond to meals that were actually delivered. The article's separate findings do point beyond paperwork: 13 SHGs had no kitchen or office at the billed address, non-member men were cooking for pay, and stock registers were missing. But those findings attach to subsets, not to the whole ₹8.1 cr.
verdicts.reason: The source says what the claim says. FPJ quotes: "54 unregistered self-help groups (SHGs) were engaged in supplying HCM in seven of the 13 test-checked districts" and "These SHGs supplied meals worth Rs 8.1 crore to 252 anganwadi centres." The amount, count, period and sample framing all match. The edge's own description correctly limits it to a sample, not a state total. The tier is right: one credible outlet reporting a named primary document (a CAG audit). It stays reported, not documented, until the CAG report PDF itself is cited. The only weakness is wording: the article says "supplied meals worth", not "paid". Payment by the DPOs is the natural reading, but it is an inference.
verdicts.corrections: 1) The lab should follow the source's wording: "54 unregistered SHGs supplied hot cooked meals worth ₹8.1 cr to 252 anganwadis (CAG test-check, 7 of 13 districts)". Alternatively, keep "paid" and add to d: "article states value of meals supplied; payment by DPOs inferred". 2) Add upgradeIf: "CAG report on establishment and functioning of anganwadi centres, MP (period to Mar 2024) located on cag.gov.in, which confirms the ₹8.1 cr and gives the government's reply", and add killIf: "report shows the ₹8.1 cr was not paid, or the SHGs were registered". 3) In benefit.how, "regulatory-moat breach" overstates what is in hand. Use "payments to groups not meeting SHG-registration eligibility norm (per CAG)". 4) Check that aggregation uses only the pmout edge (c030) and not the enforce edge c028 as well, since both carry a=8.1. 5) The URL slug typo "saven" is the publisher's own and should stay. The citation title already reads "seven".

verdicts.dateTest: Written out, the claim is: MHA (as FCRA administrator) put OSF in the prior-reference category in 2016. The date holds. The MHA affidavit quoted in the Delhi HC order of 21.02.2023 (W.P.(C) 238/2020, https://indiankanoon.org/doc/167147408/) says MHA "under section 46 of the FCRA, 2010 directed the Reserve Bank of India ... vide this Ministry's letter dated 30th May, 2016". RBI then relayed it to banks by letter DBR.AML.No.15320/14.08.001/2015-16 dated 07.06.2016, and Punjab National Bank issued a circular on 14.06.2016. The Hindu reported the listing at the time (published 2016-06-09, https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/Three-American-donors-put-under-watch-list/article14392124.ece). The Tribune piece is dated 2025-03-19 and says "2016", which matches. 'from' can be narrowed to 2016-05-30. On the relevant timeline, 13 of the 21 listed donors were added under the NDA and 8 under the UPA.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity name is loose but the node holds. The Tribune calls it "Open Source Foundation (OSF)", which is a misnomer. TOI (2025-03-19) names "Open Society Institute, US". The RBI/PNB text says MHA decided to add "Open Society Foundation (OSF), World Movement for Democracy (WMD) and National Endowment for Democracy (NED), United States of America" for not allowing credits without prior approval. The petitioner in the Delhi HC case is "Open Society Institute as registered owner of the trademark Open Society Foundations", joined by Open Society Foundation London and Foundation to Promote Open Society. The listing therefore covers the OSF network through its US legal entity (OSI), so the edge target ngo:open-society-foundations is acceptable if the node records OSI, OSF London and FPOS as covered legal entities. The actor is MHA, Foreigners Division, FCRA Wing, acting under s.46 FCRA 2010. Correct.
verdicts.baseRate: This is not discriminating as evidence of targeting OSF. In 2016, 21 foreign donors were under the prior-permission category: 8 added under the UPA and 13 under the NDA (The Hindu 2016-06-09). Two other US democracy-promotion donors, NED and WMD, were added in the same order. Ford (2015) and Compassion International and FFWPU (March 2016) were added in the same period. Among foreign donors that fund rights or advocacy work, the listing is common. The Gates Foundation and the Sangh-linked US charities are not listed, which the file already records in symmetryCheck.
verdicts.denialFound: OSF challenged the listing in court rather than denying it. OSF filed W.P.(C) 238/2020 in the Delhi HC in January 2020. It challenges the unpublished MHA/RBI circulars of 15.01.2015 and 07.06.2016 on two grounds: they were not notified in the Gazette as required by s.11(3)/46, and they reach remittances that are not foreign contribution. It also asked for the reasons for the listing and why no prior notice was given. OSF spokesperson Jonathan Birchall told The Hindu: "The Open Society Foundations confirm the filing of a petition in the Delhi High Court ... will be making no further statement on the matter" (https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/george-soros-open-society-foundations-moves-hc-against-mha/article61638640.ece). MHA's stated ground, from its affidavit: "incriminating reports from security agencies against the Open Society Foundation, which impinges on the our national security"; the material was filed in a sealed envelope. The case was still pending on 06.01.2026 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/185169269/). The court asked the Union to say whether the circulars apply only to FCRA-covered remittances and listed the matter for 15.04.2026. I did not find an OSF statement on the 2025 ED searches; my web search budget was exhausted, so this is not a finding that none exists.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine use of s.46 FCRA, which MHA has applied to about 21 foreign donors across both governments, including two other US democracy-promotion funders in the same order. The practical effect is that each remittance to an Indian association needs MHA clearance; it is not a ban. MHA says the trigger was intelligence input. The Hindu (2016) reports the alleged conduct as funding associations not registered under FCRA. No court has tested either the ground or the listing.
verdicts.reason: The underlying fact stands, but the claim's stated evidentiary position is false, and the tier depends on that position. The claim says the listing is "known only via ED's 2025 account; the order and stated ground not opened". In fact, (1) The Hindu reported it on 2016-06-09 with the co-listed donors and the "adverse intelligence inputs" ground. (2) A Delhi HC order dated 21.02.2023 in OSI v Union of India, W.P.(C) 238/2020, quotes the RBI letter of 07.06.2016 citing the MHA decision under s.46 and the MHA affidavit giving the date (30.05.2016) and the ground ("incriminating reports from security agencies ... national security"). (3) OSF confirmed its challenge on the record in 2020. A court order plus two independent credible outlets (The Hindu 2016 and TOI/Tribune 2025) meets the documented tier. The 'reported' tier and the "only via ED" framing should go, and the existing gap entry is closed by these sources.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. Restated: the ED searched eight Bengaluru premises linked to Soros' EDF/SEDF and OSF on Tuesday 18 March 2025 (a Tuesday, checked). The Tribune published at 2025-03-19T03:30+05:30 and says "The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Tuesday conducted searches at eight premises in Bengaluru". The News Minute also gives "Tuesday, March 18" and Scroll also has "on Tuesday". The 2016 prior-reference listing comes before the alleged workaround, so the order of events holds. Nothing has been adjudicated as of 2026-09. Setting the claim start date to 2025-03-18 is correct.
verdicts.identityTest: Mostly passes. Three things to note. (1) The Tribune names the wrong entity: it calls it "Open Source Foundation (OSF)" and "Economic Development Fund (EDF)". Scroll names it correctly: "the Open Society Foundations was placed under the 'Prior Reference Category' by the Ministry of Home Affairs in 2016". So ngo:open-society-foundations is the right node, but the record should say the Tribune misnamed it. (2) The reports do not show that OSF's own offices were searched. The premises named are Aspada Investments Pvt Ltd ("investment adviser-cum-fund manager of Soros Economic Development Fund (SEDF) in India", which Scroll calls "a wholly owned subsidiary of a Mauritius entity"), Rootbridge Services Pvt Ltd and ASAR Social Advisor Pvt Ltd (per TNM). No CIN is given for any of them. The edge should name SEDF/Aspada as the entity searched, and OSF as the entity the allegation is about. (3) The FDI/consultancy allegation comes from unnamed "ED sources", not an ED press release or a named officer.
verdicts.baseRate: The allegation does not single OSF out, so it tells us little about intent. The 2016 MHA prior-reference measures also hit other large foreign donors, including Compassion International (a Christian evangelical donor, not critical of the government) and, for a time, the Ford Foundation. ED FEMA searches are routine: the agency runs thousands of FEMA cases. Moving foreign money into India as FDI into for-profit companies plus consultancy fees is the normal structure for any foreign impact investor, including Omidyar, Gates-linked vehicles and SEDF. That structure only becomes a problem if the money ends up paying for NGO activity. The discriminating question is the end use, and that is exactly what has not been adjudicated. Symmetry check against the SPEC controls: I found no reporting of equivalent FEMA searches on the Indian vehicles of government-neutral or aligned foreign donors. That gap is consistent with selective enforcement, but it does not prove it.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. The Tribune, Scroll (https://scroll.in/latest/1080421/ed-raids-eight-george-soros-linked-entities-in-bengaluru) and The News Minute (https://www.thenewsminute.com/karnataka/bengaluru-ed-raids-eight-locations-linked-to-george-soros-open-source-foundation) carry no statement from OSF, SEDF or Aspada, and none says it contacted them. So in the reports I checked they were not asked. I found no statement in the OSF newsroom or in Google News results. WebSearch was over budget, so the search for a response was partial.
verdicts.innocentReading: SEDF invests in Indian for-profit companies through Aspada, which is its SEBI/RBI-regulated fund manager and wholly owned by a Mauritius entity. This is lawful FDI and can go through the automatic route. Consultancy fees paid to Indian advisory firms such as ASAR are ordinary services income. The 2016 prior-reference listing controls FCRA donations to NGOs, not FDI into companies. The funds contravene FEMA only if they can be shown to have paid for NGO activity in breach of end-use conditions. ED has asserted that through unnamed sources and has not proved it. No show-cause notice or adjudication order has been published.
verdicts.reason: The one source was opened and quoted, and it says what the claim says: the date, eight premises, FEMA, the 2016 prior-reference category, and the FDI plus consultancy-fee workaround attributed to "ED sources". Scroll and The News Minute independently confirm it. The allegation is unadjudicated and comes only from unnamed agency sources, so tier "alleged" is right for the FEMA-violation part, and there is a contra edge (c010). The fact that the searches happened would qualify as documented, since at least three outlets report it. Nothing in the chronology, the identity of the entities, or the sources refutes the claim. The weaknesses are a naming error in the source, OSF being treated as the searched entity when the premises searched were SEDF/Aspada and linked firms, and a missing innocentReading.

Add second and third sources: ["Scroll 2025-03-18","https://scroll.in/latest/1080421/ed-raids-eight-george-soros-linked-entities-in-bengaluru"] and ["The News Minute 2025-03-19","https://www.thenewsminute.com/karnataka/bengaluru-ed-raids-eight-locations-linked-to-george-soros-open-source-foundation"]. 2. In "d", note that the Tribune misnames OSF as "Open Source Foundation" and that the allegation comes from unnamed "ED sources", not an ED release. 3. Name the premises searched (Aspada Investments Pvt Ltd, Rootbridge Services Pvt Ltd, ASAR Social Advisor Pvt Ltd) and state that the reports do not show OSF's own office being searched. Consider pointing the enforcement edge at an SEDF/Aspada node and keeping OSF as the subject of the allegation. 4. Fill innocentReading: lawful FDI into for-profit companies plus consultancy fees; prior-reference controls FCRA donations, not FDI; a violation depends on unproven end use. 5. Change c010 "d" from "asked/not asked unknown" to "No response recorded; Tribune, Scroll and TNM reports carry no OSF/SEDF/Aspada comment and do not say they were contacted (not asked, per available reporting)". 6. Optionally split the fact of the searches (documented, three outlets) from the FEMA allegation (alleged). 7. Keep upgradeIf and killIf as written.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: DOGE (US executive) said on 2025-02-16 that USAID was giving CEPPS US$21m for "voter turnout in India", and cancelled it; Trump repeated it on 2025-02-19/20. The dates match the sources. Tribune (2025-02-17): "$486 million in grants to the Consortium for Elections and Political Process Strengthening" included "$21 million for 'voter turnout in India'", cancelled on Sunday 16 Feb. Business Standard (2025-02-21, 11:37 IST) gives the same date. The underlying award, however, is the 2022-07 CEPPS award for Bangladesh (Amar Vote Amar/Nagorik, July 2022 to October 2024). BS: "USAID's official records confirm that no projects funded by the Consortium for Elections and Political Process Strengthening (CEPPS) have been implemented in India since 2008." So there is no India-designated award in any window for the from=2025-02-16 edge to attach to. The ₹85/US$ conversion is also out of date. It comes from the FY2023-24 Finance Ministry report. The RBI reference rate in mid-February 2025 was about ₹86.6-87.0, which gives about ₹182 crore; Bhaskar's headline uses "₹182 cr".
verdicts.identityTest: The assertion is attributed correctly: the DOGE X post, and Trump quoted in BS as "Why do we need to spend $21 million for voter turnout in India? Wow, $21 million! I guess they were trying to get somebody else elected." The nodes are wrong as a money edge. ngo:usaid to ngo:cepps for US$21m exists only as the Bangladesh award, and c017 already records that award at the same ₹178.5 crore. c015 therefore gives the same money twice and puts the second copy in India. BS names the implementers as IFES, IRI and NDI, for Bangladesh. The venue is uncertain. BS says "speaking in Miami", but my recollection is that the "somebody else elected" line was said on 2025-02-20 at the Republican Governors Association in Washington, and the Miami FII speech on 02-19 used different wording. I could not verify this, so I am flagging it rather than asserting it. Trump's own version then changed: "$18 million going to my friend Prime Minister Modi" (Indian Express, 2025-02-24).
verdicts.baseRate: Several items in DOGE's February 2025 cancellation lists were later shown to be mislabelled or misattributed. The Washington Post (2025-02-22) ran "How a false DOGE claim ignited a political firestorm in India". A country label that is wrong in a DOGE list does not tell you much about any particular country. Symmetry: both sides used the same claim as a weapon. BJP (Amit Malviya, quoted in Tribune): "external interference in India's electoral process". Congress later used Trump's "my friend Modi" version against the BJP (Scroll, 2025-02-23). Under the same lens neither party is supported, because no money reached India. The Bangladesh control has a documented award; India has none.
verdicts.denialFound: A response exists, so c016's text is wrong. On 2025-08-21 MEA told Parliament, citing US Embassy data, that USAID gave no US$21m for voter turnout in India. My recollection is that this was a written Rajya Sabha answer by MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh, which said the Embassy's 2014-2024 USAID data showed no US$21m received and no voter-turnout activity implemented. I confirmed the event only from Google News RSS listings dated 2025-08-21/22. These headlines include the Indian Express ("Citing US embassy, Govt confirms: No $21-million USAID poll grant in India"), The Hindu ("USAID didn't receive funding of $21 million for voter turnout in India: Embassy to MEA"), NDTV ("US Embassy Contradicts Trump's 'USAID Fund For Voter Turnout In India' Claim"), The Wire ("MEA Says US Embassy Denies Trump's Claim of $21m USAID Funds to Modi, All USAID Pacts with India Ended August 15"), Scroll, TOI and BOOM. I could not open the article bodies (The Wire renders with JS; Google News links are encoded), so the MoS name and the 2014-2024 window are unconfirmed. Earlier, ThePrint (2025-03-17) reported that MEA had asked the US Embassy for details. The Washington Post (2025-02-22) called it "a false DOGE claim". I found no statement from CEPPS, IFES, IRI or NDI themselves; whether they were asked is unknown.
verdicts.innocentReading: DOGE staff labelled a line from the CEPPS award portfolio as "India" when the US$21m voter-participation award was for Bangladesh. Trump repeated the label, and the figure then drifted to "$18 million … to my friend Modi". The boring explanation is a clerical mislabel amplified by political speech, not a hidden India grant. It fits every piece of evidence: the Bangladesh award records, "no CEPPS projects in India since 2008", and the US Embassy's own data given to MEA.
verdicts.reason: Kill it as an edge; keep it as a narrative. The assertion is accurately sourced: both URLs say DOGE listed and cancelled "$21 million for 'voter turnout in India'", and BS quotes Trump. But the edge claims that USAID sent ₹178.5 crore to CEPPS for India. Its own killIf is met ("USAID award records show the only US$21m CEPPS voter-participation grant was for Bangladesh"). BS/Indian Express report it, and the asserting party's own government then withdrew it: the US Embassy told MEA, and MEA reported this to Parliament in August 2025. The claim's line "contra c016 = no CEPPS/USAID response recorded" is false, because the US government, which now administers what was USAID, did respond. Keeping the edge would also count c017's Bangladesh money twice and place it inside the India graph.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Remove the c015 money edge (s=ngo:usaid, t=ngo:cepps, pred=grant, a=178.5, benefit.amountCr=178.5). Keep c015 as a narrative or claim node labelled "DOGE/Trump assertion (2025-02-16/20), withdrawn by US Embassy data (2025-08)", with a=null, and set supersededBy to c017. 2) Rewrite c016 to record the US Embassy data given to MEA and reported to Parliament on 2025-08-21 (Rajya Sabha written answer). Denier node: US Embassy New Delhi or US government. Use the MEA Rajya Sabha Q&A page as the source, fetched from mea.gov.in or sansad.in, and use the Indian Express, The Hindu or The Wire articles of 2025-08-21/22 as secondary sources. Remove the "No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown" wording. Once the primary text is fetched, that contra is documented-tier. Also add the Washington Post 2025-02-22 item. 3) Fix the FX rate: use the RBI reference rate for 2025-02-17 (about ₹86.9/US$, roughly ₹182 crore), not the FY2023-24 FinMin rate of ₹85. Or drop the rupee figure altogether, since no money flowed. 4) Mark the "in Miami" venue as unverified: the "somebody else elected" line may be from the 2025-02-20 RGA speech in Washington. Add Trump's later "$18 million … my friend Modi" variant (Indian Express, 2025-02-24) to show the assertion was unstable. 5) Fill in innocentReading with the mislabelled-line-item explanation.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as stated: Sabrang/SACW (asserting party) say IDRF (Maryland 501(c)(3), active since the late 1980s) disbursed funds mainly to Sangh affiliates, 1994–2000. The source says: "In the years from 1994 to 2000 for which the data is available, roughly 75% of the IDRF's total disbursements (over $ 3.2 million) went to the IDRF–designated organizations." That matches the edge's from=1994 and to=2000. Footnote 36/37 cites "Annual Reports of IDRF" for 1994–2001, a minor mismatch. The report is dated 2002, and Outlook republished it on 20 November 2002. IDRF was operating across the whole window, so the date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The cited source is the full text of §4 of "The Foreign Exchange of Hate: IDRF and the American Funding of Hindutva", © 2002 Sabrang Communications & Publishing Pvt Ltd and The South Asia Citizens Web, republished by Outlook. It names IDRF throughout, the same Maryland charity as node ngo:idrf. The recipients it names are "Parivar organizations, especially those affiliated with or controlled by the RSS, the VHP and the Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA)", with Sewa Bharati and Ekal Vidyalaya named in §4.4.3. The target node "rss" is defined in the file as "RSS and its affiliates (Sangh Parivar)", so the collective target is defensible, though VKA would be more precise. The edge frames an organisational family, not a religion or ethnicity, so it passes the framing test. No EIN has been verified for IDRF, and the file's gap already records that the guessed EINs failed.
verdicts.baseRate: It is normal, not unusual, for a US diaspora religious charity to fund service networks of its own faith. Christian charities do the same through church partners (the Compassion and World Vision controls), and so do Muslim and Sikh diaspora charities. The share going to Hindu or Sangh bodies is therefore not discriminating by itself. The only discriminating evidence is inside the report: IDRF-designated funds went more than 80% to the Sangh, but "only 10% of the donor-designated funds were earmarked for Sangh charities." That contrast rests on the report's own coding of recipients (Appendix H), which the HVK rebuttal disputes. The symmetry test gives the same result: the lens that reads Sangh-affiliated service work as political funding also reads church-affiliated service work as conversion funding (narrative 5). The file's symmetryCheck and narrative already record this, and in both cases the conclusion rests on inferences from who the grantees are, not on any adjudicated finding.
verdicts.denialFound: HVK / Ashok Chowgule rebuttal, opened at https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html. Its §1.1 summarises the report as saying "because IDRF provides donations to some of the social service projects started by the Hindutva organisations, IDRF is funding the violence". It attacks the authors' agenda ("conclude first and then get the data"), "guilt by association" and "perverting the data" (§1.5). It does not dispute that money flows to Sangh-run service projects. What it disputes is the characterisation and the method. IDRF's own November 2002 "pure concoction" statement and the 2003 six-academic rebuttal (letindiadevelop.org returns 403) were not opened. WebSearch was exhausted this session, and idrf.org's current site shows nothing about the report. No evidence shows whether IDRF was asked before publication.
verdicts.innocentReading: IDRF's founders and officers had Sangh links, and in rural and tribal India the largest Hindu-oriented networks that run schools and tribal welfare (VKA, Sewa Bharati, Ekal) are Sangh affiliates. A diaspora charity picking its own grantees would send money to networks it knows and trusts. On the report's own figures, about 70% of IDRF funds went to education and about 15% to relief. Both ends of the flow were lawful and declared, and no tribunal has found that IDRF money paid for violence. The "Sangh-affiliated" coding is the critics' own classification.
verdicts.reason: The cited source was opened and it supports the core edge as an allegation by a named party: "A vast majority (in excess of 80%) of the IDRF designated funds were sent to Parivar organizations, especially those affiliated with or controlled by the RSS, the VHP and the Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA)." Alleged is the right tier. The only primary is the critics' report, the rebuttal disputes its coding, and IDRF's schedules have not been opened. A contra (c024) exists, as the tier requires. The HVK rebuttal concedes that the flow exists and contests the characterisation. The edge is not refuted, but the claim text contains a false caveat. It says the "83%" figure is "from secondary summaries, not verified in the primary text". The primary text at the cited URL states it: "None of the organizations funded can be identified with any minority community, though 8% (in addition to the 83% that are Sangh affiliated) are clearly identifiable as Hindu or Jain religious organizations." The d field's "Amount not stated in the section opened" is also wrong, because the section states "over $ 3.2 million". The claim also overstates scope. The 80–83% applies to IDRF-designated funds, about 75% of disbursements. Donor-designated funds were 10% Sangh. Combining the two gives roughly 65% of total disbursements. That still counts as "predominantly", but as the claim's own inference, not the source's sentence.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Claim text and d: delete "the '83%' figure is from secondary summaries, not verified in the primary text". Replace it with a note that §4.1 of the primary text republished by Outlook gives ">80% of IDRF-designated funds to Parivar organisations (RSS, VHP, VKA)" and "83% … Sangh affiliated". Flag that it is unclear whether the 83% is a share of organisations or of funds; Figure 2 is titled "Percentage Distribution of IDRF Funds By Ideology". 2. d: replace "Amount not stated" with: "IDRF-designated disbursements 1994–2000: 'roughly 75% of the IDRF's total disbursements (over $3.2 million)'". Note that the parenthetical could refer to either the 75% slice or the total. 3. Scope: change "IDRF disbursements went predominantly" to "IDRF-designated disbursements (~75% of total) went >80% to Sangh affiliates; donor-designated only 10% (report's coding, Appendix H)". Also record IDRF's 10% allocation to VKA on donor-designated gifts of $1,000 or more. 4. Recipient list in d: VKA, RSS and VHP affiliates in §4.1; Sewa Bharati, Ekal Vidyalaya and Bharat Kalyan Pratisthan (~$86,000) in §4.2–4.4. 5. Fill innocentReading with the lawful same-network service-funding reading above. 6. c024 contra: add the HVK summary sentence showing the rebuttal concedes the flow and disputes the "funds violence" characterisation; the contra URL can point to https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html. 7. File-level: update the gap at ~line 2173–2174 ("Narrative 6's numerators (83% …) are recorded from secondary readings only"), narrative 6's strongestCounter ("The 83% figure is unverified here") and the gaps list line ~2439. The 83% is now read in the primary text via Outlook; only its scope (organisations vs funds) is unresolved. 8. Optional: consider an ngo:vka target node instead of or alongside the collective "rss" node. benefit.amountCr stays null unless a dated USD→INR conversion is recorded.

verdicts.dateTest: Sewa International Inc (EIN 20-0638718, Sugar Land TX, IRS ruling 2004-08) existed across the whole period, so its tenure fits. The report's Sewa window is 2005–2019, not 2001–19. The 2001–19 span belongs to the seven-group total. ThePrint's article (Vandana Menon, 2022-06-14) and the report (dated 2022-05-23 on DocumentCloud) both fall inside the claim window. The date test passes, with the Sewa span needing correction to 2005–2019.
verdicts.identityTest: ThePrint, the only cited source, does not name Sewa International among the seven charities. Its one mention of Sewa is in a separate sentence about the 2021 Al Jazeera Covid-relief story: "five Right-wing groups — Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of USA, HAF, Infinity Foundation, Sewa International, and VHPA — received $833,000 of U.S. federal Covid relief funds". Sewa's membership of the seven comes only from the primary report, 'Hindu Nationalist Influence in the United States, 2014-2021' (Jasa Macher/SACW), Table 4: "Sewa International | Sevabharati Keralam | $17.1 million (2005-2019) | $12.9 million". The report's footnote 322 cites Sewa International's Form 990s, which matches the US entity (EIN 20-0638718). The node identity holds. The target node "rss" is not in either source. The only Indian recipient the report names for Sewa is Sevabharati Keralam, labelled "(Selected)", with no amount.
verdicts.baseRate: The seven were chosen for their Sangh affiliation, so 100% of them share the property by construction and the figure tells you nothing on its own. Across US faith-based diaspora charities that fund India, most send money to service networks of the same religion. The SPEC controls World Vision, Compassion and Missionaries of Charity send money through church partners, and Muslim diaspora charities send it through co-religionist bodies. On the evidence here, "a faith-based US charity funds a co-religionist service network in India" does not set Sewa apart. What would set it apart is a documented transfer to an RSS affiliate, and the report names only one selected recipient with no amount.
verdicts.denialFound: None found from Sewa International USA. ThePrint says: "ThePrint has reached out to the organizations mentioned in this article for their comments on the report." Sewa is mentioned in the article, so it was presumably asked, but no Sewa reply was published. HAF ("All the allegations [in this report] about HAF are baseless") and HSS ("a politically motivated smear campaign") replied for themselves only. Sewa's About page calls it "a Hindu faith-based, humanitarian, nonprofit service organization" that "serves humanity irrespective of race, color, religion", but it does not address the report.
verdicts.innocentReading: The report's Sewa figure comes from Form 990 Part III row 4e (2008–2019), which is total program service expenses. That covers Sewa's US work (disaster relief such as the Harvey response, refugee and Covid programmes) as well as work abroad, and it is not a record of grants to India. The report admits this: "a group did not appear to differentiate consistently between programs in the U.S. from those in India, and further investigation is needed to disaggregate the funding." ProPublica totals for Sewa's expenses in 2014–2018 come to about $9.7m, in line with the report's $12.9m for 2014–19. That suggests the $17.1m is close to all of Sewa's spending everywhere, not money sent to India. The report's own author also says "most of [these actions] are legal". The boring explanation is that this is a US Hindu faith-based relief charity with some Indian partners, and board members with HSS roles.
verdicts.reason: As written, the edge fails in three places. (1) The cited source (ThePrint) does not say Sewa is one of the seven; only the primary report does, so the source chain is only partly confirmed. (2) The record says "Amount not stated for Sewa alone", but the report gives $17.1m (2005–2019) and $12.9m (2014–19). (3) Most importantly, the edge Sewa → rss with the predicate "grant" is a conjunction that no source states. The report's figure is total program expenses, not grants. It says "much"/"some" went to India without splitting US from India spending, and the only Indian recipient it names is Sevabharati Keralam, with no amount; RSS is never named. Chaining "Sewa spent $17.1m" + "some went to India" + "recipient is Sangh-linked" into "Sewa granted money to RSS" is exactly the pattern the rubric forbids. As a narrative, "a pseudonymous SACW-facilitated report alleges Sewa is one of seven Sangh-affiliated charities that spent $158.9m", it survives at alleged, with a contra.
verdicts.corrections: t: change "rss" to a Sevabharati Keralam node (or a generic "Sangh-affiliated recipients in India, unspecified"). Do not keep an edge to rss. pred: "grant" → "program-expense (alleged, India share undisaggregated)" or similar. The record must not imply Sewa gave money to RSS. srcs: add the primary report https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/22041101/20220523_hninfluenceusa.pdf (Table 4, p.21; fn 321–322).
